title: What Is Fertilizer? Definition, Types, Components and Examples with Pictures
metaTitle: Fertilizer Definition: Types, Components and Examples
metaDescription: Fertilizer definition in plain words: what fertilizer is, how to say it, what is inside the bag, how it feeds plants, and the main types with pictures.
excerpt: Fertilizer is any material, natural or factory made, that supplies the nutrients plants need to grow, usually through the soil. That is the usual international definition, and Philippine law says much the same. Its main nutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, the three numbers on every bag. anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, adds them up for your crop with its NPK Plus Calculator.

blocks.text: This guide covers the word, the bag, the types with photos and a short history. For which bag suits which crop, see [fertilizer for plants](/blog/fertilizer-for-plants).

items: Fertilizer is plant food: it supplies nutrients the soil lacks.
Say it FUR tuh ly zer. In Tagalog, it is abono or pataba.
The three numbers on a bag are percent nitrogen, phosphate and potash.
Main types: inorganic, organic, biofertilizer, water soluble, controlled release.
Every fertilizer sold in the Philippines must be FPA registered.

blocks.text: Fertilizer definition: what the word means

Merriam Webster defines fertilizer as a substance, such as manure or a chemical mixture, used to make soil more fertile. The usual international definition is wider: any chemical or natural material that provides nutrients to plants, usually through the soil, but also through leaves or paddy water.

In the Philippines, the legal fertilizer definition comes from Presidential Decree 1144 of 1977. It covers any substance, organic or inorganic, applied to the soil to promote growth, raise yield or improve quality. So the fertilizer meaning, in farm words, is plant food you add because the soil alone falls short.

blocks.caption: Fertilizer definition in brief
rows: FUR tuh ly zer, stress on the first part

blocks.text: Fertilizer pronunciation, synonyms and the word in Tagalog

Merriam Webster gives the fertilizer pronunciation as FUR tuh ly zer. The most common fertilizer synonym is plant food. In Tagalog, fertilizer is abono or pataba, and most farmers say abono. Our [farm words in Tagalog](/blog/farm-words-in-tagalog) list has more.
Fertilizer components: what is inside the bag?

Every bag shows three numbers, the grade: the percent of nitrogen (N), phosphate (P2O5) and potash (K2O), in that order. So a 50 kg bag of complete 14 14 14 holds 7 kg of each. Each fertilizer name on a bag pairs a common name, such as urea, with its grade.

Behind those numbers sit fertilizer ingredients such as urea, ammonium phosphate and potassium chloride. The University of Georgia notes that phosphate times 0.44 gives actual phosphorus, and potash times 0.83 gives potassium. The rest of the weight is secondary nutrients, the other parts of each compound, and in some products filler for easier spreading.

blocks.caption: Fertilizer components: the nutrients plants need
rows: The three grade numbers on every bag
Zinc, boron, iron, manganese, copper, molybdenum, chlorine and others

blocks.text: The fertilizer effect on plant growth
Plants need these nutrients to build leaves, roots and grain, and the one in shortest supply holds growth back. Here is what each does in rice.

items: **Nitrogen** speeds growth and raises yield through more tillers, leaf area and grain filling. Without enough, plants stay small and yellowish green.
**Phosphorus** builds roots and drives tillering, flowering and ripening. Without enough, plants are stunted and dark green.
**Potassium** strengthens roots, helps prevent lodging and raises resistance to pests and diseases. Without enough, older leaves brown at the tips and edges.

blocks.alt: A 1942 test field with signs reading Starved by lack of plant food and Nourished on phosphate and lime, showing the fertilizer effect on plant growth
blocks.caption: A 1942 test field: one side starved of plant food, the other fed phosphate and lime. Tennessee Valley Authority, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

blocks.text: More is not always better. The international fertilizer code warns against overuse as well as underuse, since nitrogen and phosphorus lost from fields pollute water.
Fertilizer types, with pictures

Fertilizer types differ in where they come from and how they work. The FPA list of registered fertilizers, updated September 15, 2026, sorts products by type, including biofertilizer, biostimulant and controlled release fertilizer.

From plants and animals, slow, builds soil
Living microbes that fix nitrogen or free up nutrients
Dissolves fully, for leaf sprays or drip lines

Inorganic fertilizer

Inorganic fertilizer is what most farmers mean by abono. Straight fertilizers like urea carry one main nutrient, while compound and blended fertilizers carry two or three. A compound comes as round granules of one color. A bulk blend, like the one at the top of this page, mixes different granules, so it shows several colors.

Read our guides to [urea 46 0 0](/blog/urea-fertilizer), [complete 14 14 14](/blog/complete-fertilizer-14-14-14), [16 20 0](/blog/16-20-0-fertilizer), [ammonium sulfate 21 0 0](/blog/ammonium-sulfate-21-0-0), [potash](/blog/potash-fertilizer) and more [inorganic fertilizer examples](/blog/inorganic-fertilizer-examples).

blocks.text: Organic fertilizer

Organic fertilizer comes from plants and animals. It is carbon rich, made from manure, compost, vermicompost and similar materials. The Philippine standard, PNS/BAFS 183:2023, asks it for 5 to 10 percent total NPK. Our [organic fertilizer examples](/blog/organic-fertilizer-examples) show how to make and use each one.

blocks.alt: A heap of dried cow dung piled for use as organic fertilizer
blocks.caption: Cow manure, an organic fertilizer. Compost it before use on food crops. Photo by Yahuzaishat, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

blocks.alt: Long piles of compost made from crop waste lying in a field
blocks.caption: Compost piles made from crop waste. Photo by SuSanA Secretariat, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

blocks.text: Biofertilizer

A biofertilizer carries living or dormant microbes, such as bacteria, fungi or algae. They fix nitrogen from the air or free up soil nutrients. For rice in the Philippines, Azospirillum bacteria and the water fern azolla are the best known. Their gains are real but modest, as our page on [organic vs inorganic fertilizer](/blog/organic-vs-inorganic-fertilizer) explains.

blocks.alt: Green cyanobacteria grown in a glass flask for use as a biofertilizer
blocks.caption: Blue green algae, a biofertilizer that fixes nitrogen from the air. Photo by Joydeep, CC BY SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

blocks.text: Water soluble, foliar and controlled release fertilizer

Water soluble fertilizer dissolves completely, so it can be sprayed on leaves or sent through a drip line. Leaves take in only small amounts, so a spray only tops up the soil program. See our [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer) guide.

Controlled release fertilizer has a coating on each granule that lets nutrients out slowly. It costs more per kilo of nutrient, so it suits pots and nurseries more than a hectare of palay.

blocks.alt: Pink water soluble NPK 19 19 19 fertilizer powder in a dish
blocks.caption: Water soluble NPK 19 19 19 powder for leaf sprays and drip lines. Photo by Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

blocks.text: Fertilizer clipart and an easy drawing for school

Students often need a picture of fertilizer for school work. A simple, easy fertilizer drawing for a poster is a sack with its grade on the front, such as 14 14 14. Clipart of a fertilizer sack works the same way, and the photos here show the real thing.
A short history of fertilizer
Farmers used manure, ash and compost long before anyone measured why they worked. Fertilizer science is much younger.

blocks.caption: Milestones in fertilizer history
rows: Lawes and Gilbert start the Broadbalk experiment at Rothamsted, England. One strip has had no fertilizer since
Fritz Haber wins the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for making ammonia from its elements, the base of urea
A long term continuous rice cropping experiment starts in Los Baños, Laguna
Presidential Decree 1144 creates the FPA and requires fertilizer registration
An international code of conduct on fertilizer use comes out
The Philippines updates its organic fertilizer standard, PNS/BAFS 183:2023

blocks.text: What fertilizer research shows today

Long experiments still teach the most. Broadbalk's unfertilized strip shows what the soil gives on its own. Since 1968, a field in Los Baños has grown three rice crops a year while testing four nitrogen rates. Closer to the farm, fertilizer research turns into bag plans and product trials, which our page on [rice growth enhancers](/blog/rice-growth-enhancers) reviews.

blocks.text: Questions about fertilizer

items.q: What is fertilizer for plants, in simple words?
items.a: It is plant food. Fertilizer adds nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and other nutrients that the soil cannot supply in full.

items.q: What is the fertilizer definition in Philippine law?
items.a: Presidential Decree 1144 defines fertilizer as any substance, organic or inorganic, applied to the soil to promote growth, raise yield or improve quality. It must be FPA registered before sale.

items.q: What do the numbers on a fertilizer bag mean?
items.a: They are the percent of nitrogen, phosphate and potash. A 50 kg bag of 16 20 0 holds 8 kg of nitrogen, 10 kg of phosphate and no potash.

items.q: How do you say fertilizer in Tagalog?
items.a: Abono or pataba. Most farmers say abono, as in abono para sa palay.
